section.title: Circumcision and Passover at Gilgal
section.sectionRationale: Before a single battle is fought, God halts the army to attend to worship and covenant. The generation born in the wilderness is circumcised, receiving the covenant sign their fathers had neglected; then Israel keeps the Passover in the land for the first time, and the manna ceases as they eat the produce of Canaan. It is one movement, the covenant renewal that must come before the conquest, teaching that the land is entered as a covenant people, not merely a conquering one.
section.thesis: God will not let Israel go to war until they are marked as His covenant people and have remembered His redemption, so He rolls away the reproach of Egypt through circumcision and Passover, and quietly ends the wilderness era as the manna stops and the promised land begins to feed them.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the kings' hearts melt and the new generation is circumcised, verses 1 to 9; the Passover kept in the land, verses 10 to 11; and the manna ceasing as Israel eats the produce of Canaan, verse 12.

units.label: The new generation circumcised
units.note: today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt

verses.text: Now when all the Amorite kings west of the Jordan and all the Canaanite kings along the coast heard how the LORD had dried up the waters of the Jordan before the Israelites until they had crossed over, their hearts melted and their spirits failed for fear of the Israelites.
At that time the LORD said to Joshua, “Make flint knives and circumcise the sons of Israel once again.”
So Joshua made flint knives and circumcised the sons of Israel at Gibeath-haaraloth.
Now this is why Joshua circumcised them: All those who came out of Egypt, all the men of war, had died on the journey in the wilderness after they had left Egypt.
Though all who had come out were circumcised, none of those born in the wilderness on the journey from Egypt had been circumcised.

For the Israelites had wandered in the wilderness forty years, until all the nation’s men of war who had come out of Egypt had died, since they did not obey the LORD. So the LORD vowed never to let them see the land He had sworn to their fathers to give us, a land flowing with milk and honey.
And He raised up their sons in their place, and these were the ones Joshua circumcised. Until this time they were still uncircumcised, since they had not been circumcised along the way.
And after all the nation had been circumcised, they stayed there in the camp until they were healed.
Then the LORD said to Joshua, “Today I have rolled away the {{cherpah|reproach}} of Egypt from you.” So that place has been called Gilgal to this day.

units.label: The Passover kept in the land
units.note: they kept the Passover on the plains of Jericho

verses.text: On the evening of the fourteenth day of the month, while the Israelites were camped at Gilgal on the plains of Jericho, they kept the {{pesach|Passover}}.
The day after the Passover, on that very day, they ate unleavened bread and roasted grain from the produce of the land.

units.label: The manna ceases
units.note: that year they ate the crops of Canaan

verses.text: And the day after they had eaten from the produce of the land, the {{man|manna}} ceased. There was no more manna for the Israelites, so that year they began to eat the crops of the land of Canaan.

cherpah.gloss: Reproach, disgrace, scorn. The LORD says He has rolled away the reproach of Egypt from Israel. The reproach may be the shame of slavery and of the wilderness generation's unbelief, or the taunt that God brought them out only to let them die; renewing the covenant sign of circumcision removes it, marking them afresh as God's own people, no longer a byword but a nation set apart to Him.

pesach.gloss: Passover, from the root to pass over. The feast commemorating the night the LORD passed over the blood-marked houses in Egypt and spared Israel's firstborn, Exodus 12. Kept now in the land for the first time, it roots the conquest in redemption: the people who take Canaan are the people God redeemed by the blood of the lamb, and the feast points forward to Christ our Passover, 1 Corinthians 5:7.

man.gloss: Manna, the bread from heaven that fed Israel through forty years in the wilderness, Exodus 16. Its ceasing marks the end of the wilderness era: God's provision does not stop but changes form, from miraculous desert bread to the ordinary produce of the promised land. The God who fed them by miracle now feeds them through the harvest of the inheritance He gave.

basic.context: Israel has crossed the Jordan and the Canaanite kings are paralyzed with fear, yet God does not send Israel straight into battle. Instead He tells Joshua to attend to the covenant first. The whole generation born during the forty years in the wilderness had never been circumcised, the sign God gave Abraham that marked Israel as His people. So they are circumcised, and God says He has rolled away the reproach of Egypt from them. Then, healed and marked, they keep the Passover in the land for the first time, remembering the exodus. The very next day they eat the produce of Canaan, and the manna that had fed them for forty years stops. The question underneath is: what kind of people does God bring into His promises?
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative recording covenant acts. Circumcision was the old covenant sign given to Abraham; the New Testament teaches that it pointed to a deeper circumcision of the heart, and that believers are marked out now not by the flesh but by faith and the Spirit, so we do not reinstate the physical rite. What endures is the truth the passage dramatizes: God's people belong to Him by covenant and are grounded in redemption before they are sent to serve.
basic.originalLanguages: God rolls away the cherpah, the reproach, of Egypt through the covenant sign. Israel keeps the pesach, the Passover, in the land, rooting the conquest in redemption. And the man, the manna, ceases as the promised land begins to feed them, the wilderness era quietly ending.
basic.typology: Circumcision points to the circumcision of the heart accomplished in Christ, and Passover points to Christ our Passover Lamb, whose blood spares us from judgment. The manna, bread from heaven, points to Jesus, the true bread from heaven who gives life to the world. All three signs at Gilgal find their fulfillment in Him.
basic.christ: Israel keeps the Passover just as they are about to receive the land, grounding everything in the blood of the lamb; Christ is our Passover, sacrificed for us. The manna that sustained them points to Jesus, who says, I am the bread of life. And the circumcision of the flesh points to the true circumcision, the putting off of the flesh, that comes through Christ.
basic.god: God is the covenant Lord who insists on being related to as such. He is patient, raising up a new generation after the old fell in unbelief, and gracious, rolling away their reproach. He is the faithful provider, changing manna for harvest without ceasing to feed His people. And He is the redeemer whose Passover stands at the foundation of all He does with Israel.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 17 gives circumcision as the covenant sign to Abraham. Exodus 12 institutes the Passover. Exodus 16 records the manna in the wilderness. Colossians 2 speaks of the circumcision made without hands in Christ. And John 6 presents Jesus as the true bread from heaven.
basic.oneStory: Before the conquest, God renews His covenant with Israel, marking them as His own and grounding them in the redemption of the Passover, while the wilderness manna gives way to the fruit of the promised land. Each sign, circumcision, Passover, and bread from heaven, points forward to Christ, in whom God's people are truly marked, redeemed, and fed.

context.literary:
Five short time markers chain the whole unit together, at that time, verse 2, the tenth day of the month, verse 10, the day after, verse 11, and the day after that, verse 12, compressing an entire covenant renewal, a national religious festival, and the end of a forty year food supply into what reads almost like a liturgical calendar rather than an ordinary narrative report. The tight sequencing matters: the narrator wants readers counting days, because the events are inseparable from their timing, healing has to happen before Passover can be kept, verse 8, and Passover has to be kept before the land's produce can be eaten, verse 11, each step a precondition for the next.

The chapter also completes a literary frame that opened back in chapter 2. There the king of Jericho's messengers heard that Israel's approach made hearts melt, and Rahab told the spies that all who dwell in the land are melting in fear, verses 2:9 and 2:11. Here, almost word for word, all the Amorite and Canaanite kings hear of the Jordan crossing and their hearts melt and their spirits fail, verse 1. That repeated language brackets chapters 2 through 5 as a single literary movement, the approach to the land, before the fighting itself begins in chapter 6; only after this frame closes, with Israel circumcised, fed by covenant food, and confronted by the commander of the LORD's army, does the first battle actually start.
context.historical:
Circumcision was not unique to Israel in the ancient world; later classical writers report that the Egyptians also practiced it, so Israel's mark was not distinguished by the physical act itself but by the covenant God attached to it, given to Abraham as a sign of a specific promise, Genesis 17:11, not a general rite of passage or hygiene practiced by whichever nation adopted it. What made circumcision distinctly Israel's own was never the knife, it was the God who commanded it and the promise it sealed.

The flint knives, verse 2, are a notable detail on their own. By this period Israel had access to bronze tools, yet the text specifies flint, an older and more deliberate choice; the same detail appears earlier when Zipporah circumcises her son with a flint knife at a moment of covenant crisis, Exodus 4:25, suggesting flint carried a traditional, perhaps sacred association with this particular rite that metal tools did not share, an older way of cutting reserved for this one covenant sign even after newer technology existed for everything else.

The place name itself preserves the memory bluntly: Gibeath haaraloth, the hill of the foreskins, verse 3, almost certainly named for the literal heap left behind after a whole generation of men were circumcised in one location, an earthy, unflattering detail that a later editor concerned only with propriety might have been tempted to soften, yet the text keeps it exactly as it happened, tied permanently to the ground itself.
context.canonical:
Long before Joshua reaches this hill, Moses had already looked past the physical rite to something the knife alone could never accomplish: circumcise your hearts, therefore, and stiffen your necks no more, Deuteronomy 10:16, and further ahead still, the LORD your God will circumcise your heart and the hearts of your descendants, so that you may love the LORD your God with all your heart and all your soul, Deuteronomy 30:6, a promise of inward transformation Moses himself says still lies in Israel's future even as he speaks. Jeremiah presses the same point on a later, unfaithful generation, circumcise yourselves to the LORD, and remove the foreskin of your hearts, Jeremiah 4:4, treating the outward sign as worthless if it never reaches the heart it was meant to represent.

Gilgal's circumcision therefore sits at the midpoint of a long canonical argument: the sign is real, commanded, and necessary, Exodus 12:48 already made it a precondition for keeping Passover at all, yet the sign was never the whole of what God wanted, only the visible half of a promise whose inward half Moses could already see coming and Jeremiah could already see being ignored. The New Testament resolution, a circumcision of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter, whose praise is not from man but from God, Romans 2:28 to 29, does not discard what happens at Gilgal so much as complete the very trajectory the Torah had already set in motion, generations before Christ.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Any Israelite reader of this passage already knew the story of Shechem, where Simeon and Levi exploited the very vulnerability of newly circumcised men to slaughter a city while it was still sore and unable to defend itself, Genesis 34:25. The author places Israel's own new generation in exactly that position, freshly circumcised and healing, verse 8, on the very edge of hostile Canaanite territory, with Jericho's walls in plain sight, and does not flinch from how reckless this looks by any military logic.

That deliberate echo is the point: the author wants readers to feel the danger before he tells them nothing came of it, so that trust in God's protection, rather than in Israel's own readiness or strength, becomes unmistakable. He also wants Israel to see itself accurately in this moment, not as a battle hardened army finally arriving to claim what it had earned, but as a people who still needed correcting, marking, and feeding by God before they could be trusted with a single battle, so that whatever victories follow in the coming chapters will be read correctly, as gifts to a covenant people rather than the rewards of a conquering one.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The specific timing, at this exact geographic and military moment, before Jericho and not at any other point in Israel's history, is part of the historical record and not a pattern to schedule around; nothing requires that spiritual renewal always precede a specific external accomplishment in a fixed order. What is rightly drawn out is the principle beneath the timing: God is willing to delay strategic advantage in order to deal first with His people's standing before Him, and He is willing to name and remove a reproach His people carry, whether from past failure, past slavery, or past shame, before sending them further.

That principle applies without requiring a physical rite or a specific ritual calendar; Paul tells the Corinthians who once lived in various sins that they were washed, sanctified, and justified, and such were some of you, but now, 1 Corinthians 6:9 to 11, describing exactly this kind of decisive removal of a former reproach before a new commission begins.

debates.question: What is the reproach of Egypt that God rolled away at Gilgal?

views.label: The shame of slavery and the wilderness generation's unbelief
views.case: Israel had been slaves in Egypt and then a nation under judgment, dying in the desert for unbelief and lacking even the covenant sign; renewing circumcision and keeping Passover in the land removes that whole history of disgrace, marking a fresh start for the redeemed people now entering the promise.

views.label: The taunt that God could not finish what He began
views.case: The reproach may be the mockery of the nations, that the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt only to kill them in the wilderness, Numbers 14:16; by bringing this generation across the Jordan and re-establishing the covenant, God silences that taunt and vindicates His faithfulness.

debates.bearing: Either way, the rolling away of the reproach declares that God has decisively restored His people to covenant standing and is fulfilling His promise, so they enter the land not in shame but as those He has claimed and vindicated.

debates.question: Why was circumcision suspended for the entire forty years in the wilderness?

views.label: The sign withheld from a generation under judgment
views.case: The LORD had vowed that the entire generation of men who came out of Egypt would die in the wilderness for their unbelief, verse 6 and Numbers 14:22 to 23; some read the suspension of circumcision as fitting that judgment, since applying the covenant sign to a generation already sentenced to die outside the promise would have made the sign itself an empty formality rather than a living pledge.

views.label: A practical hardship of the journey
views.case: Others read the suspension more simply, as one more difficulty of forty years of constant movement through hostile and unpredictable terrain, where the vulnerability of a healing wound, so starkly illustrated at Shechem, Genesis 34:25, made the rite genuinely dangerous to perform along the way, so that it waited for the settled pause Gilgal finally provided.

debates.bearing: Whichever explanation carries more weight, the text itself gives no excuse, only a fact, and treats the renewal at Gilgal not as correcting a minor oversight but as the deliberate closing of a whole generation's unfinished covenant standing before the new generation could go to war as God's marked people.

study.originalLanguages:
Beyond cherpah, pesach, and man, the chapter's Hebrew carries several more details worth slowing down for. The command to circumcise the sons of Israel again, verse 2, is literally shuv, return, joined to the verb for circumcising, a common Biblical Hebrew construction that uses the verb return to mean do again, do a second time, rather than any actual movement back and forth; the BSB's own footnote catches this, rendering it literally again, the second time. The wording signals that this is a renewal of a covenant practice temporarily set aside, not the invention of a brand new rite, since the nation had genuinely been circumcised once, at the exodus generation's own beginning, even though the wilderness born sons in front of Joshua now had never personally received it.

The verb behind healed, verse 8, is rapha, the ordinary word for healing throughout the Old Testament, and also the root behind one of the LORD's covenant names, I am the LORD who heals you, Exodus 15:26, spoken to Israel not long after the exodus. That the newly circumcised nation simply waits, unable to march or fight, until healing has run its course, places the whole army briefly and deliberately under the same dependence any sick or wounded individual Israelite would feel toward the God who heals, a vulnerability the text does not rush past.

The place name Gilgal itself carries a wordplay the footnote to verse 9 confirms, sounding like the Hebrew root galal, to roll; the LORD says today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt, using this same rolling language, so that the location's very name becomes a permanent pun preserving the theological claim made there. The same root elsewhere describes rolling a heavy stone off a well's mouth, Genesis 29:3 and 29:10, a small but suggestive echo, since here too something heavy and long settled, a generation's disgrace, is rolled off and away in a single decisive act.

Finally, the word today, hayyom, verse 9, deserves attention on its own. Moses uses the same word again and again in Deuteronomy to mark the day of decisive covenant renewal, today I command you, Deuteronomy 8:11, this day the LORD has declared you to be a people for His own possession, Deuteronomy 26:18; Joshua's use of today at Gilgal belongs to that same vocabulary of decisive, dateable covenant moments, treating the renewal at Gilgal not as a vague spiritual improvement but as a specific day Israel could point back to exactly as they would later point back to the day at Sinai or the day of the covenant renewal at Shechem, Joshua 24:25.

typology.type: Circumcision, the covenant sign in the flesh
typology.fulfillment: Circumcision cut away a small piece of flesh as the visible sign that an Israelite male belonged to the LORD by covenant; Paul describes something the knife could never reach, a spiritual circumcision, the putting off of the body of the flesh, in the circumcision of Christ, Colossians 2:11, which he explicitly contrasts with a circumcision performed by human hands. He tells the Romans that real circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit, not the letter, and that its praise comes from God rather than from other people, Romans 2:28 to 29. The type is genuinely fulfilled rather than merely echoed, since the very language of cutting away and putting off carries straight from the physical rite into the spiritual reality; where it still falls short as a picture is that the old sign could be received by an infant with no faith of his own, while the new reality Paul describes always comes joined to personal faith in the risen Christ.

typology.type: The Passover kept as Israel enters the land
typology.fulfillment: Israel keeps this Passover with unleavened bread and roasted grain from the land itself, verse 11, the first time the feast is kept on the very soil it was always aimed toward, closing the loop between a promise made in Egypt and a promise now being kept in Canaan. Paul tells the Corinthians plainly, Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed, therefore let us keep the feast, 1 Corinthians 5:7 to 8, treating the Passover not as an old ceremony replaced by a new one but as a shadow whose substance has finally arrived. Peter adds that believers were redeemed with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot, 1 Peter 1:18 to 19, drawing the Passover lamb and the crucified Christ into the same picture. The type is complete in one sense, the blood truly saves, yet it still awaits its final feast, the marriage supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:9, where redemption is not merely remembered but fully enjoyed.

typology.type: The manna ceasing as the land provides
typology.fulfillment: The manna's ceasing is stated with almost clinical plainness, there was no more manna for the Israelites, verse 12, a food that had fallen every morning for forty years simply stopping the day ordinary bread became available. Jesus takes up the very memory of that manna when crowds who had just been fed bread ask Him for a sign, and He answers, your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, yet they died; I am the bread of life, John 6:48 to 49 and 6:58, drawing a deliberate contrast between food that sustained a body for a lifetime and food that gives life forever. The type is real but limited, since manna, however miraculous, still had to fall daily and still left those who ate it mortal; the bread Jesus offers is not renewed daily because it never runs out and never needs replacing, satisfying a hunger the wilderness generation's manna, for all its wonder, could never finally reach.

typology.type: The reproach of Egypt rolled away from Israel at Gilgal, Joshua 5:9
typology.fulfillment: Israel's shame, carried since slavery and sharpened by a whole generation's failure in the wilderness, is publicly and decisively removed in a single stated act, today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you. The writer of Hebrews describes Jesus enduring the cross, scorning its shame, Hebrews 12:2, and urges believers to go to Him outside the camp, bearing the reproach He bore, Hebrews 13:12 to 13, reversing the direction of this type: at Gilgal reproach is rolled away from God's people, but at the cross Christ takes reproach onto Himself so that it need never rest on His people again. The type is not a simple repetition but an inversion that completes the picture, since Israel's reproach was removed by a rite performed on their own bodies, while the church's reproach is removed because Christ bore it in His own body once for all.

study.christ:
Everything in this passage happens before Israel fights, and that order carries the weight of the gospel itself. God does not tell Israel to conquer first and get right with Him afterward; He insists on covenant identity, redemption remembered, and dependence proven through a costly, vulnerable wait, before the first battle of the conquest is even attempted. That order matches exactly how the New Testament describes the Christian life: you also must count yourselves dead to sin but alive to God in Christ Jesus, and only then, therefore do not let sin reign, Romans 6:11 to 12. Grace and identity come first; obedience and effort follow from what has already been settled, never the reverse. Gilgal is the Old Testament's own object lesson in that order.

The immediate sequel to this passage, just beyond its final verse, shows Joshua meeting a man with a drawn sword who identifies Himself as commander of the army of the LORD, Joshua 5:14, and Joshua falls facedown in worship. The timing is not incidental: only after circumcision, Passover, and the ceasing of the manna has fully marked Israel as a covenant people, ready to depend rather than to presume, does the true commander of the coming battle reveal Himself. Many readers across church history, without inventing new claims about the passage, have recognized in this figure a preview of Christ Himself, present with His people at the very edge of the fight, receiving the worship no mere angel would accept. Whether or not that identification is pressed further, the timing agrees with everything Gilgal has just taught: victory belongs to the commander, not to the army, and the army's first task is always worship, not weaponry.

Every element of Gilgal, in other words, refuses to let Israel imagine its coming victories as its own. The covenant sign, the redemption feast, and the changed food supply all insist that a people entering into promised rest do so as those already marked, already redeemed, and already fed by grace, a pattern the gospel simply completes when it insists that everything a believer does in Christ's name follows a work already finished rather than earns a status still to be won.
study.god:
Verse 6 says plainly that the LORD vowed the wilderness generation would not see the land, using the identical language of a sworn, binding oath that describes His promise of the land to their fathers in the very same verse. God's word of judgment and God's word of promise rest on the same footing, His own sworn character, so that the reader is meant to trust the promise precisely because the judgment was so exactly and so unflinchingly carried out; if God kept His hard word to the fathers' generation to the letter, His kind word to their sons can be trusted every bit as firmly, since neither oath depends on anything but who God is.

This is also a God whose care changes shape without ever lapsing. Manna was never an end in itself, a permanent replacement for ordinary provision, but a specific gift matched to a specific season of helplessness, when Israel could grow nothing and store nothing in the wilderness. The instant the land can feed them, God lets the miracle stop, without warning or ceremony, verse 12 records it almost in passing, because provision was always the point, not any one particular form provision happened to take. A God who can feed a nation by bread that falls from the sky can feed the same nation, without missing a step, from ordinary soil, and expects His people to recognize His hand in the ordinary as readily as they recognized it in the miraculous.

Finally, this is a God unwilling to send even the most obviously favored generation into danger unmarked and unfed. The men before Joshua had done nothing to deserve their fathers' judgment and nothing yet to earn their coming victories; they simply inherit a promise their fathers forfeited. God's first act toward them, before any battle, is to mark them as His own and feed them at His own table, showing that belonging to God's people has never run on personal merit accumulated in advance, only on being brought, however undeservedly, into a covenant kept by someone else's faithfulness.

crossReferences.note: The original terms of the covenant sign specify every male, every generation after Abraham, including those born in the household, must be cut off from the people if the mark is missing, terms this whole wilderness born generation had been quietly failing to meet.

Only the circumcised may keep the Passover, so the whole nation had to be circumcised before it could keep the feast, which is exactly the order of events at Gilgal, circumcision first and Passover immediately after.
Christ our Passover has been sacrificed for us, therefore let us keep the feast; the feast Israel keeps for the first time in the land points ahead to a sacrifice still centuries future.

Jesus declares Himself the true bread from heaven, greater than the manna that fed and yet could not keep alive the fathers who ate it in the wilderness; the ceasing of manna at Gilgal points to Him who gives eternal life.

Paul tells believers they were themselves circumcised in Christ, a cutting away performed by no human hand at all, buried with Him in baptism and raised through faith in the power that raised Jesus from the dead.

Simeon and Levi had once exploited the vulnerability of newly circumcised men to slaughter Shechem while its men were still in pain, a memory that makes Israel's own choice to be circumcised at the edge of hostile territory here look reckless by ordinary military sense, and trustworthy only if God Himself is guarding them.

Moses had already promised that the LORD would one day circumcise Israel's heart so they would love Him fully; the physical renewal at Gilgal marks the sign faithfully kept even while the deeper, promised reality Moses described still lay ahead of this generation.

God reveals Himself soon after the exodus as the LORD who heals you; the days Israel spends healing from circumcision before Passover, verse 8, place the whole nation briefly and visibly under exactly that name and character.

Believers are called to go to Jesus outside the camp, bearing the reproach He bore, reversing the picture at Gilgal where reproach is rolled away from Israel; at the cross Christ instead takes reproach onto Himself so His people never have to carry it again.

study.oneStory:
Genesis opens with humanity placed in a garden already bearing God's own image, provided for before a single work was required of them; the fall broke that order, and ever since, the temptation has been to imagine standing before God, or before any calling He gives, on the strength of achievement rather than gift. Gilgal quietly restores the original order at the threshold of the conquest: God marks Israel as His covenant people and feeds them by grace before He sends them to do anything at all. The land is entered by a people already identified as God's own, not a war band earning identity through victory.

The whole Old Testament keeps circling back to this order and this place. Israel returns to Gilgal repeatedly in the centuries after Joshua, for judging, Samuel's ministry, and the confirming of a king, evidence that this pattern, mark and feed before you send, remained a touchstone for a nation prone to reverse it and to trust instead in armies, alliances, or its own righteousness, exactly the temptation Deuteronomy 9:4 to 5 warns against.

The New Testament completes the pattern rather than abandoning it. Believers are marked by a circumcision made without hands and fed at a table Christ Himself provides before they are sent anywhere to do anything for Him, so that mission always follows identity and never earns it. And the manna theme itself does not end at Gilgal; the risen Christ promises the one who overcomes hidden manna, Revelation 2:17, a food kept by God for His people beyond anything the wilderness generation ever tasted, still future, still a gift, still evidence that the God who fed Israel by bread from heaven and then by the fruit of Canaan has not run out of ways to provide. Gilgal stands, in the middle of Israel's story, as proof that entering what God has promised has always depended on being already His, marked, redeemed, and fed, long before the fighting starts.

quiz.q: Why did the new generation of Israel need to be circumcised at Gilgal?

options.text: Those born in the wilderness had never received the covenant sign, so they were marked as God's people before entering the land.
options.note: Verses 4 to 7 explain the whole wilderness generation was uncircumcised until now.

options.text: Circumcision was a medical requirement before battle.
options.note: It had nothing to do with medicine; it was the covenant sign given to Abraham.

options.text: It was a punishment for the sins of their fathers.
options.note: It was not a punishment but the restoration of the covenant sign to the new generation.

options.text: The Canaanites demanded it as a condition of surrender.
options.note: The Canaanites had no part in it; it was God's command to mark His covenant people.

quiz.q: What did God say He had done for Israel at Gilgal?

options.text: He had rolled away the reproach of Egypt from them.
options.note: Verse 9 gives this as the meaning of the covenant renewal and the name Gilgal.

options.text: He had given them permanent peace from all enemies.
options.note: Battles still lay ahead; what God did here was roll away their reproach, not end all war.

options.text: He had made them wealthier than the Canaanites.
options.note: The point was covenant standing and removed disgrace, not wealth.

options.text: He had cancelled the covenant made with Abraham.
options.note: The opposite: He renewed the covenant sign, He did not cancel the covenant.

quiz.q: What significant change happened to Israel's food supply?

options.text: The manna ceased once they ate the produce of the promised land.
options.note: Verse 12 marks the end of the wilderness manna as the land begins to feed them.

options.text: God sent a double portion of manna to celebrate the crossing.
options.note: The manna did not increase; it stopped, as the land's harvest took its place.

options.text: They ran out of food entirely and had to fast.
options.note: They did not go hungry; they simply ate the crops of Canaan instead of manna.

options.text: They returned to eating the food of Egypt.
options.note: They ate the produce of Canaan, the promised land, not the food of Egypt.

quiz.q: Why did God attend to circumcision and Passover before the fighting began?

options.text: So Israel would enter the land grounded in covenant and redemption, as God's people, not merely as an army.
options.note: The passage roots the conquest in covenant renewal and the Passover before any battle.

options.text: So the soldiers would be too weak to disobey orders.
options.note: They did rest to heal, but the purpose was covenant and redemption, not weakening the troops.

options.text: Because the Canaanites had asked for a delay.
options.note: No delay was requested; God halted them to renew the covenant, not at the enemy's request.

options.text: Because God had changed His mind about giving them the land.
options.note: God had not changed His mind; He was preparing His covenant people to receive the promise.

quiz.q: How do the signs at Gilgal point to Christ?

options.text: Passover points to Christ our Passover, the manna to Jesus the bread of life, and circumcision to the circumcision of the heart in Him.
options.note: All three signs find fulfillment in Christ, 1 Corinthians 5:7, John 6, Colossians 2:11.

options.text: They show that God's people are saved by keeping rituals in the flesh.
options.note: The signs are real, but they point beyond themselves to Christ; salvation is by faith in Him, not the rites themselves.

options.text: They teach that physical circumcision is still required of Christians.
options.note: The New Testament fulfills circumcision in the heart through Christ; the physical rite is not reinstated.

options.text: They have no connection to Christ or the gospel.
options.note: Passover, manna, and circumcision all clearly point forward to Christ.

questions: God rooted the conquest in redemption by having Israel keep the Passover first. How does remembering that you belong to God by redemption shape the way you approach the tasks He gives you?
God rolled away the reproach of Egypt and gave His people a fresh start. What past shame or failure do you need to entrust to the God who rolls reproach away in Christ?
The manna stopped when the land began to provide, yet God's care never lapsed. Where are you tempted to think God has stopped providing, when really His provision has only changed form?
God halted a whole army to attend to covenant and worship before battle. Are there ways you rush into activity and service while neglecting your relationship with God?
Passover, manna, and circumcision all point to Christ, our Passover, our bread of life, and our true circumcision. How does seeing Jesus in these signs deepen your love for Him this week?

translationNotes.note: Circumcise the sons of Israel once again renders a phrase the BSB footnote gives literally as again the second time; it refers to renewing the practice for the new generation, not repeating it on individuals.
Gibeath-haaraloth means the hill of the foreskins, as the BSB footnote notes, naming the place of the circumcision.
Gilgal sounds like the Hebrew for roll, as the BSB footnote notes, tying the name to God rolling away the reproach of Egypt.
